turns.prompt_text: What frequency do walkie talkies typically operate at the ones that go up to like 40 mi as advertised
turns.response_html:
Those consumer walkie-talkies that claim a "35-mile" or "40-mile" range typically operate in the UHF (Ultra High Frequency) band, specifically on FRS (Family Radio Service) and GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service) frequencies.

They use 22 shared channels that sit right between 462 MHz and 467 MHz.

Here is how those frequencies break down under the hood, and the reality behind that 40-mile claim:

The Frequencies & Services

  • Channels 1–7 & 15–22: Operate on the 462 MHz main and interstitial channels.
  • Channels 8–14: Operate on the 467 MHz interstitial channels (which are strictly limited to low-power 0.5-watt transmissions).

The radios themselves usually cross-label these channels. If you buy a standard blister-pack walkie-talkie from a sporting goods store, it is likely an FRS radio (license-free, maxing out at 2 watts on the high-power channels) or a hybrid GMRS radio (which can push up to 5 watts on a handheld, or 50 watts on a mobile base station, but technically requires an FCC license to operate).

The Reality of the "40-Mile" Claim

The 40-mile range advertised on the box is a line-of-sight calculation under perfect, absolute vacuum-like conditions—typically measured from the top of a mountain peak to a flat valley below with zero obstructions.

Because UHF radio waves travel via line-of-sight and don't bend over the horizon or easily penetrate dense matter, physical obstacles drastically cut your range:

EnvironmentRealistic Expected Range
Dense Woods / Neighborhoods0.5 to 1.5 miles (trees and buildings absorb the 462 MHz signal)
Open Fields / Flat Terrain2 to 5 miles
Mountain Peak to Mountain Peak20 to 40+ miles (true line-of-sight)

If you want to stretch closer to those massive distances without climbing a peak, you have to look into GMRS repeaters. Higher-end GMRS radios can transmit on special repeater input channels (the 467 MHz main frequencies), hitting an antenna mounted high on a commercial tower or mountain that rebroadcasts your signal across the region.

turns.prompt_text: How does this compare with a Wi-Fi antenna?
turns.response_html:
When you compare a 462 MHz walkie-talkie signal to a standard Wi-Fi antenna, it essentially comes down to a classic engineering trade-off: range vs. bandwidth.

Because Wi-Fi operates at vastly higher frequencies, the way the waves behave, interact with obstacles, and carry data is entirely different.

The Frequency and Wave Physics

The standard frequencies for Wi-Fi are 2.4 GHz ($2400\text{ MHz}$), 5 GHz ($5000\text{ MHz}$), and the newer Wi-Fi 6E/7 6 GHz ($6000\text{ MHz}$) bands.

Because of the inverse relationship between frequency and wavelength ($\lambda = \frac{c}{f}$), the physical size of the radio waves matters immensely for how they move:

  • Walkie-Talkie (462 MHz): Has a wavelength of about 65 cm (2 feet). Waves this size are relatively robust. They can easily curve slightly over small hills, pass through drywall, and pass around trees or vehicles without being completely scattered.
  • Wi-Fi Antenna (2.4 GHz / 5 GHz): Has a wavelength of about 12 cm (4.7 inches) for 2.4 GHz, and just 6 cm (2.3 inches) for 5 GHz. These tiny waves are highly susceptible to attenuation (fading). They struggle to penetrate solid objects like brick, concrete, or metal, and can even be absorbed or scattered by heavy foliage or human bodies.

Antenna Design and Power

The hardware design itself is tailored to these different wavelengths:

  • Form Factor: A walkie-talkie needs a relatively long whip antenna (often a "rubber ducky" antenna, which is a coiled wire inside a rubber sheath) to effectively match that 65 cm wavelength. A Wi-Fi antenna can be incredibly small—often just a tiny trace printed directly onto a circuit board or a small internal patch module.
  • Radiation Patterns: Walkie-talkie antennas are strictly omnidirectional along the horizontal plane to catch signals from any direction while moving. Wi-Fi uses both omnidirectional antennas (like the sticks on a home router) and advanced MIMO (Multiple-Input Multiple-Output) arrays that use beamforming to dynamically target specific devices.
  • Power Constraints: A consumer walkie-talkie can blast up to 2 to 5 watts of power to push a signal over miles. A standard indoor Wi-Fi router is heavily restricted by the FCC, typically maxing out at 1 watt (and client devices like phones usually transmit at just 0.1 watts), which naturally limits the range to a few hundred feet.

Data Capacity vs. Range

The ultimate difference is what the signal is carrying:

FeatureWalkie-Talkie (FRS/GMRS)Wi-Fi Antenna
Frequency$\sim 462\text{ MHz}$$2.4\text{ GHz}$ / $5\text{ GHz}$ / $6\text{ GHz}$
Channel Width$12.5\text{ kHz}$ to $25\text{ kHz}$ (Very narrow)$20\text{ MHz}$ to $160\text{ MHz}$ (Extremely wide)
PayloadAnalog or low-bitrate digital voice onlyHigh-speed, high-density packet data
Primary LimitationEarth's curvature / terrain obstaclesSolid walls / atmospheric attenuation

Because a Wi-Fi channel is thousands of times wider than a walkie-talkie channel, it can carry gigabits of data per second, but it exhausts its energy incredibly fast. The walkie-talkie channels are tiny, focused straw-holes of bandwidth: they can't stream video, but that narrow focus allows the signal to punch through the noise across vast distances.
